reasons: Hand-maintained data with no check that it matches the projects.

terms.meaning: A hand-written description of a project that overrides or adds to what a scan finds.
A short name used in web addresses and file paths for a project.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Purpose of the spec file
sections.what: A header explaining that this file holds the extra links, AI features and full stacks that the scan cannot provide.
sections.why: The header states that AI features come from each build's write-up and that full node lists are used for repositories not scanned locally.
sections.watch_out: Facts here are not checked against the projects, so update them by hand when a project changes.

sections.name: specs (part 1)
sections.title: Extra parts and features for early projects
sections.what: For several projects, lists extra technologies, extra links, technologies to remove and AI feature descriptions. The abacus entry gives a full hand-written technology list.
sections.why: Lets each project's diagram show parts that the code does not reveal.
sections.watch_out: Removals match by exact ID or label, so a renamed technology will quietly stay on the diagram.

sections.name: specs (part 2)
sections.title: Project architecture maps, part two
sections.what: Holds written descriptions of four projects: groundwork, watchtower, needle and the first part of blueprint. Each project lists its parts with a short id, a label and a category, then the links between parts, then a short list of features. This part does not draw or run anything; the page that reads this data is not in the packet.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. It is plain data, so it is probably read by a page that draws the diagrams and feature lists.
sections.watch_out: Each link names parts by their short ids, and this file does not check that those ids exist, so a typo would quietly break that link.

sections.name: specs (part 3)
sections.title: Project architecture maps, part three
sections.what: Continues the same kind of project data: the rest of blueprint, then yardstick, first-draft, digital-twin and the start of pulse. The digital-twin entry has the longest feature list, and yardstick has an empty one.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The same likely reason as the earlier part applies: a page reads these entries to show each project.
sections.watch_out: Yardstick has an empty feature list, so anything that expects at least one feature may show a blank section for it.

sections.name: specs (part 4)
sections.title: Project architecture maps, part four
sections.what: Finishes the pulse entry and adds haus-nous, the last project. The closing brace at the end finishes the whole data object, so any new project must be added inside it, above that brace.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. Keeping every project in one object lets a reader look them up by name.
sections.watch_out: A missing comma or bracket in this area would likely stop the whole file from loading, which would affect every project, not only the one edited.

summary: Hand-written extras for each project: extra technologies, extra links, technologies to remove, and AI features.
purpose: Adds what the code scan cannot see, such as AI features and models in projects that are not scanned.
why: The header says AI features come from each build's write-up, and full stacks are written here for repositories not scanned locally.
how: Each project key holds optional lists. stack-graph.mjs reads them and adds or removes items from the scanned result.
inputs: None. This file is data only.
outputs: The specs object, which stack-graph.mjs imports.
risks: Must be updated by hand when a project changes. A drop entry matches by exact ID or label, so a renamed technology stays on the diagram. A mistyped project key silently gets no extras.
debug: If a project diagram lacks an expected item, check the project key spelling and the drop list.
